meta.blurb: Amara has to design a science project about food, and her grandfather Kofi used to be a cook. Together they sort the real evidence from the hype about which foods help the body look after itself.
meta.bible: Amara: a schoolgirl of about fourteen who is choosing a science project; curious and sensible, and she likes to ask what the evidence is. Kofi: her grandfather, a retired Cook who ran a small restaurant; warm, funny and practical. Mrs Okoro: Amara's science teacher. The book runs over about eight weeks, from the day Amara picks her project to the school Science Fair, in Kofi's kitchen, the market and the school hall. The project is a Protection Plate: a plate of everyday foods that may help the body look after itself. Key ideas: the body already protects and repairs itself, through the Skin, the Immune system and the repair of cells; food supports these jobs but is not a cure; observational studies show links, not proof; trials give stronger evidence; the whole pattern of eating matters more than one Superfood. Foods: Berries, Anthocyanins; leafy greens, Vitamin K, Warfarin; Broccoli, Cabbage, Cruciferous vegetables; Tomatoes, Lycopene; Onions, Garlic; Beans, Lentils, Fibre; Oats, Beta-glucan, whole grains; Nuts; Olive oil; Oily fish, Omega-3; Yoghurt; Tea; Turmeric, Curcumin; Cocoa, Flavanols; frozen vegetables. A large Mediterranean diet trial in Spain found fewer heart problems in people given extra olive oil or nuts. The World Health Organization advises at least 400 grams of fruit and vegetables a day, free sugars under ten percent of energy, and under five grams of salt a day; its cancer agency in 2015 classed processed meat as a cause of bowel cancer and red meat as a probable one. Trials of high-dose Beta-carotene pills in people who smoked found more lung cancer, not less. Alcohol raises the risk of several cancers. Charred and burnt food can form harmful compounds. Safety facts: nut allergies can be serious; vitamin K foods matter to people who take warfarin; anyone with a health condition, a pregnancy, a child to feed or on medicine should ask a doctor or registered dietitian. This book is general information and is not medical advice. Voice and tone: warm, clear and a little funny; honest about uncertainty; no invented numbers, studies or quotes; no diagnosis and no personal treatment advice.

B1B2: Amara has to choose a project for her science class, and any topic is allowed. She picks food, because she wants to know whether some foods really help the body look after itself.
Her grandfather Kofi ran a small restaurant for thirty years, and he offers to help with the project. He says he has fed thousands of people, but he has never studied what is inside the food.
Before they talk about food, Kofi reminds her that the body already looks after itself. When she cuts a finger, the skin closes and heals, and many of the body's cells are replaced all the time.
Kofi says that food supports the body's own protection, but it is not a cure. Even a very healthy eater can become ill, because age, genes, infections and luck all play a part.
At school, Mrs Okoro explains how scientists learn about food. They follow large groups of people for many years and see who becomes ill, so they can find links, but a link is not proof.

In a trial, people are given different foods on purpose and then compared. This gives stronger evidence, but trials are expensive, they are often short, and it is hard to make people keep to one diet for years.
Kofi says there is no single superfood that protects you by itself. What matters most is the whole pattern of what you eat over many years, and that pattern is made of ordinary meals.

At the market, Kofi shows her the bright colours of fruit and vegetables. Plants contain thousands of natural substances, and some of them may help the body, although scientists are still learning how.
Berries get their deep colour from natural substances called anthocyanins. Some studies link eating berries with a healthier heart, but the effect is modest, and berries are not a miracle.
Dark leafy greens such as spinach and kale are rich in vitamins, minerals and fibre. Large studies link eating them often with a lower risk of heart disease.
Leafy greens are rich in vitamin K, which helps blood to clot. People who take a medicine called warfarin need to keep their greens steady and should ask their doctor or pharmacist about it.

Broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower and sprouts belong to one plant family and contain natural sulphur compounds. Studies link eating more of them with a lower risk of some diseases, but the evidence is not yet certain.
Some vitamins escape into the water when vegetables are boiled for a long time. Steaming, quick stir-frying or eating some raw keeps more of them.
Tomatoes are red because they contain a natural substance called lycopene. The body takes in more of it from cooked tomatoes, especially when a little oil is added.
Onions and garlic are the start of countless cooked dishes around the world. Some studies link them with better health, but the evidence for garlic on its own is mixed.
Beans, lentils and chickpeas are cheap, filling and rich in fibre and protein. Eating them regularly is linked with a lower risk of heart disease and diabetes.

Oats contain a fibre called beta-glucan, which can help to lower cholesterol. Whole grains such as oats, brown rice and wholemeal bread are linked with a lower risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes.
Nuts contain healthy fats, fibre and protein, and a small handful a day is linked with a lower risk of heart disease. They are rich in energy, so a handful is enough.

Nut allergies can be serious and even dangerous, so nuts must never be given to anyone who is allergic. Parents of young children should ask a doctor or a health visitor before they start to give nuts.

A large trial in Spain looked at the Mediterranean way of eating. People who were given extra olive oil or nuts had fewer heart problems than a comparison group, although scientists still discuss the details.
Oily fish such as salmon, sardines and mackerel contain omega-3 fats. Many health guides suggest eating fish twice a week, including one portion of oily fish.
Eggs are an affordable source of protein and vitamins. For most healthy people, eating eggs in moderation fits well into a healthy diet.
Yoghurt and other fermented foods such as kimchi contain live microbes. Some small studies suggest benefits for health, but the research is still young.
Black and green tea contain plant substances called polyphenols. Studies link drinking tea with a slightly lower risk of some diseases, but only when it is not loaded with sugar.
Turmeric is a yellow spice that contains a substance called curcumin. Results in laboratory dishes look exciting, but the evidence in people is weak, because the body takes in very little curcumin.
Cocoa contains plant substances called flavanols, and some small studies show a small effect on blood pressure. Chocolate also contains sugar and fat, so it is a treat and not a medicine.
Frozen and tinned vegetables can be as nutritious as fresh ones, and they are cheap and last longer. They count towards the daily total, so a freezer full of peas is a good thing.
Water is the best everyday drink for most people. Sugary drinks add a lot of sugar to the diet and are linked with weight gain and tooth decay.
The World Health Organization advises that free sugars should be less than ten percent of daily energy. Sugar hides in many foods, so reading labels helps.
The World Health Organization advises adults to eat less than five grams of salt a day. Herbs, spices, garlic and lemon can add flavour without more salt.

In 2015 the cancer agency of the World Health Organization classed processed meat, such as bacon and ham, as a cause of bowel cancer. It also said red meat is a probable cause, so these foods are best eaten in small amounts.

Ultra-processed foods are made mostly from industrial ingredients and often contain a lot of sugar, fat and salt. Studies link eating a lot of them with poorer health, although scientists are still studying why.
Alcohol raises the risk of several cancers, and health organisations say that drinking less is better for health. Old stories that a little wine is good for you are now disputed.
When starchy food or meat is burned or charred, harmful substances can form. It is better to cook food gently and to cut away any black parts.
Pills cannot copy everything that real food contains, such as fibre. Most healthy people who eat a good variety of foods do not need vitamin pills.
Two big trials gave high doses of beta-carotene pills to people who smoked. To the scientists' surprise, those people got more lung cancer, not less.
Some people do need supplements, such as vitamin B12 for people who eat no animal foods. A doctor or a registered dietitian can say what is right for you.
Whole fruit keeps its fibre and makes you feel full. Juice has the sugar but not the fibre, so drink only a small glass.
Words like superfood and detox on a package are marketing, not science. A real health claim needs good evidence, and the body already cleans itself with the liver and kidneys.
The ingredient list starts with what there is most of. Looking at sugar, salt and portion size on the label helps you to choose.
Food is only one part of staying healthy in the long run. Moving every day, sleeping well and not smoking all help to protect the body as well.
Eating with family and friends can make meals slower and more enjoyable. A healthy pattern is easier to keep when it is pleasant.
Young children often refuse a new food several times before they accept it. Patience and very small tastes work better than pressure or bribes.
Healthy eating does not need to be costly for ordinary families. Beans, oats, frozen vegetables, cabbage and carrots are all cheap, and fruit in season costs less.
When you cook at home, you choose what goes into the food. You control the salt, sugar and fat, and you often spend less money.

Amara designs her Protection Plate: half vegetables and fruit, a quarter whole grains, and a quarter beans, fish or other protein. She tries it with her family for a week and writes down what happens.
At the school Science Fair, Amara presents her project to teachers, parents and other students. Her honest rules about evidence, written in big letters, stand in the middle of the board.
A judge asks Amara whether these foods really prevent disease. She answers honestly that they may lower the risk for many people, but they give no guarantee.
Amara's project wins a prize for honest science, and Kofi is proud of her. On the way home he says that he has learned something too.
This book is general information and is not medical advice. If you have a health condition, an allergy, a pregnancy or a child to feed, ask a doctor or a registered dietitian first.
C1C2: Amara stared at the project sheet from her science teacher, Mrs Okoro, which said that any topic would do as long as the evidence was honest. Food seemed the most interesting choice, since everyone eats it and everyone has an opinion about it. She wanted to find out which foods truly help the body look after itself.

Amara's grandfather, Kofi, had run a small restaurant for thirty years, and when she told him about the project he put down his spoon and offered his help at once. He confessed that he had fed thousands of people without ever studying what their dinners were doing inside them. It was never too late to learn, he declared, and he rummaged for a notebook of his own.

The first thing Amara learns is that the body is not helpless, and that food is not a rescue team arriving from outside. A cut finger closes by itself, an infection is fought by the immune system, and countless cells are quietly repaired or replaced every single day. The real question, then, is whether the right foods help these natural jobs to go well.

Food, Kofi says, supports the body's own defences, and that is a much smaller promise than the advertisements make. Even people who eat very well can fall ill, because age, genes, infections and plain luck all play their part. Amara writes this at the top of her notebook in capital letters, so that she will not forget it when the exciting claims begin.

At school, Mrs Okoro explains that much of what we know about food comes from following large groups of people for many years and noting who stays well. Such studies show links between foods and health, but a link is not proof, because people who eat a lot of vegetables may also exercise more and smoke less. Amara adds a second line to her notebook: always ask what else could explain it.

Kofi tells her that a trial is a stronger kind of test, because people are given different foods on purpose and the groups are then compared. Trials are expensive and often short, though, and it is very hard to persuade hundreds of people to follow one diet for ten years. Good science, he says, usually weighs both kinds of evidence together and trusts the answer only when they agree.

Kofi snorts when Amara reads out a headline about a miracle berry, and he reminds her that the word superfood is a marketing word and not a scientific one. What seems to matter most is the whole pattern of what people eat across many years, which is built from ordinary meals rather than from one magic ingredient. A good pattern is a bit like a good team, he adds, because nobody wins alone.

At the market on Saturday morning, Kofi walks her slowly past the red peppers, the purple cabbages and the orange carrots, as though he were showing her paintings. Plants make thousands of natural substances that give them their colours and protect them from insects and sunlight, and some of these substances may help the human body too. Scientists are still learning how much they matter, he cautions, so Amara should not expect a simple answer.

Blueberries, strawberries and blackcurrants are rich in anthocyanins, the pigments that give them their deep red, blue and purple colours. Studies of large groups link regular berry eating with a slightly lower risk of heart problems, although the effect is modest and cannot be separated entirely from other healthy habits. Amara decides that berries belong on the plate, but only as one member of a large family.

Kofi cooks spinach the way he did in the restaurant, in a hot pan with a little oil and garlic, until it collapses into a glossy green heap. Dark leafy greens are rich in vitamins, minerals and fibre, and large studies link eating them often with a lower risk of heart disease. They are also cheap, he notes with satisfaction, which is a kind of health benefit of its own.

Leafy greens are rich in vitamin K, which helps the blood to clot, and this matters to anyone who takes a blood-thinning medicine called warfarin. Such patients are usually told to keep their intake of greens fairly steady rather than to avoid them, and they should always ask a doctor or pharmacist for advice. Amara writes a note on her plan that food can interact with medicine, and that a book is never a substitute for a professional who knows your health.

Broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower and Brussels sprouts belong to one plant family, and they contain natural sulphur compounds that give them their sharp smell and slightly bitter taste. Several large studies link eating more of these vegetables with a lower risk of certain diseases, including some cancers, although the evidence is not conclusive and the size of any effect is uncertain. Kofi says that the smell of boiled cabbage has probably done more damage to its reputation than science ever will.

Some vitamins dissolve in cooking water, so a vegetable that is boiled for a long time and then drained can lose a good share of them. Kofi recommends steaming, quick stir-frying or a short simmer in a little water that can be used again in a soup, and he also likes some vegetables raw. Amara tries the broccoli bright green and slightly crunchy, and it is the first time she has ever asked for a second helping.

Tomatoes owe their red colour to a pigment called lycopene, and studies link eating tomatoes and tomato products with a lower risk of some diseases, although the evidence is not strong enough to call it proof. Cooking breaks the tomato's cells open, and a little oil helps the body absorb the lycopene, so a simple sauce is better than it looks. Kofi, who made tomato sauce every morning for thirty years, accepts the praise modestly.

Kofi begins nearly every dish with an onion, and he points out that onions and garlic form the base of cooking in dozens of countries. They contain natural sulphur compounds, and some studies link them with better health, but the evidence for garlic taken by itself, especially as a pill, is mixed. Amara reflects that it is easier to enjoy something in a stew than to swallow it as a supplement.

Beans, lentils and chickpeas are among the cheapest foods in any shop, and they are rich in fibre, protein and minerals. Studies link eating them regularly with lower cholesterol and a lower risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes, and they fill people up for a very small cost. Kofi serves a lentil stew that tastes so rich that Amara suspects him of cheating.

Oats contain a fibre called beta-glucan, which has been shown in trials to lower cholesterol a little when eaten regularly. Whole grains such as oats, brown rice and wholemeal bread keep the outer layers of the grain, and large studies link them with a lower risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes. Kofi has eaten porridge every morning since he was a boy and says nobody has ever been able to talk him out of it.

Almonds, walnuts, hazelnuts and peanuts contain healthy fats, fibre, protein and minerals, and eating a small handful a day is linked with a lower risk of heart disease. Because they are also rich in energy, a handful is a good amount and a whole bag is not, and salted or sugar-coated nuts are a much weaker bargain. Amara adds a small drawing of a handful to the margin of her plan.

Nut allergies can be serious and sometimes dangerous, and Amara's classmate Tobi must carry emergency medicine at all times. Nuts must never be offered to anybody who is allergic to them, and parents of very young children should ask a doctor or a health visitor for advice before introducing them. Amara adds a line to her plan that a food that is excellent for one person can be a danger to another.

In a large trial in Spain, thousands of people at high risk of heart disease were asked to follow a Mediterranean way of eating, with extra olive oil or extra nuts, and were compared with a group given other advice. The first group had fewer heart attacks and strokes, although scientists still debate some details of how the study was run. Kofi says that his grandmother, who cooked with olive oil every day, would have been very pleased.

Oily fish such as salmon, sardines and mackerel are rich in omega-3 fats, and eating them is linked with a lower risk of heart disease. Many health guides suggest two portions of fish a week, one of them oily, although a few kinds of fish contain too much mercury for young children and pregnant women. Kofi grills sardines on the little stove in the yard and quietly admits that the smell fills the street.

Eggs are an affordable source of protein, vitamins and minerals, and they were once blamed for raising the risk of heart disease because the yolk contains cholesterol. Newer research suggests that for most healthy people, eating eggs in moderation is not a problem, although people with certain health conditions should follow the advice of their own doctor. Kofi cracks two into a pan and points out that a cheap egg is hard to beat.

Yoghurt, kefir, kimchi and sauerkraut are made with the help of living microbes, and some of those microbes survive until the food is eaten. Small studies suggest that such foods might help health in modest ways, but the research is still young, and not every product on the shelf contains many live microbes. Amara notes that this is an exciting area, as long as people remember how little is certain.

Black and green tea both contain plant substances called polyphenols, and several large studies link regular tea drinking with a slightly lower risk of heart disease and stroke. The effect is small, and it disappears into the sugar if a person adds several spoonfuls to every cup, so water, tea and coffee without sugar are the sensible drinks. Kofi pours a second cup and says that, at the very least, tea gives a person a reason to sit down.

Turmeric is a bright yellow spice, and its main substance, curcumin, has produced exciting results in laboratory dishes and in animals. Human trials are much less convincing, partly because the body absorbs very little curcumin, and so the headlines have run far ahead of the evidence. Kofi says that turmeric makes a lovely curry, and that a lovely curry is a good enough reason to use it.

Cocoa contains plant substances called flavanols, and a few small studies suggest that they may lower blood pressure slightly. Most chocolate bars, however, contain too much sugar and fat for that to matter, and the darker varieties are only a modest improvement on the sweeter ones. Amara decides that a square of dark chocolate is a pleasure and not a prescription, and that this is perfectly fine.

Fruit and vegetables are usually frozen within hours of being picked, which locks in most of their vitamins, and tinned beans and tomatoes are also nutritious, cheap and always ready to use. They count towards the daily total just as well as fresh produce, so a freezer full of peas is nothing to be embarrassed about. Kofi says that his best restaurant soups were often made from vegetables that he had saved by freezing them.

Water is the simplest and cheapest drink, and it contains nothing that the body needs to be protected from. Sugary drinks, by contrast, add a large amount of sugar without making a person feel full, and they are linked with weight gain, tooth decay and a higher risk of type 2 diabetes. Amara counts the sugar in her favourite fizzy drink and is shocked to find that it is the same as several spoonfuls.

The World Health Organization advises keeping free sugars, which are the sugars added to food and drinks or found in honey and juice, under ten percent of daily energy, and less would be better still. Sugar hides in sauces, cereals and yoghurts as well as in sweets, so reading labels is a useful habit. Kofi admits that in his restaurant days he often added more sugar than he needed, simply because people liked it.

The World Health Organization advises adults to eat less than five grams of salt a day, since too much salt raises blood pressure in many people. Most salt comes from bread, sauces and ready meals and not from the shaker on the table, and herbs, spices, garlic and lemon can make cooking taste excellent without it. Kofi tastes his food before he adds any salt, which, he says, is a habit that every cook should learn.

In 2015 the cancer agency of the World Health Organization classed processed meat, such as bacon, ham and sausages, as a cause of bowel cancer, and red meat as a probable cause. The risk to any one person from a small portion is low, which is why most guides suggest keeping these foods occasional and modest, not forbidding them. Kofi nods slowly and says that he understands, though he will miss his Sunday bacon.

Ultra-processed foods, such as packaged snacks, sweetened cereals and many ready meals, are made mostly from industrial ingredients and are usually high in sugar, fat or salt. Large studies link eating a lot of them with poorer health, although scientists are still working out how much of that is caused by the foods and how much by other parts of life. Amara decides that the safest rule is simply to cook more meals from simple ingredients.

For years, people repeated that a glass of red wine was good for the heart, but newer research has cast doubt on that comfortable idea. Alcohol raises the risk of several cancers, and health organisations advise that the less a person drinks, the lower the risk becomes. Kofi, who never drank much himself, says that he feels thoroughly vindicated and just a little smug about it.

When starchy food such as toast or potatoes is cooked until it is dark brown, and when meat is charred over a flame, harmful substances can form. The amounts that we eat are small, and the risk from a single burnt piece of toast is tiny, but it is sensible to cook gently, to aim for golden rather than black, and to cut away the burnt parts. Kofi hates waste, so he sighs deeply as he scrapes the toast over the bin.

Amara wonders whether a pill could replace all those vegetables, and Kofi tells her that it cannot, because food contains fibre and thousands of other substances that a tablet does not. Most healthy people who eat a good variety do not need vitamin pills, although some groups, such as pregnant women, may be advised to take particular ones by their doctor. Amara decides that supplements are a topic for her doctor and not for a science project.

Beta-carotene is the orange pigment in carrots, and studies had shown that people who ate lots of carrots seemed to have less lung cancer. Two big trials then gave high doses of beta-carotene pills to people who smoked, and, to the researchers' surprise, those people developed more lung cancer instead of fewer. The lesson, Kofi says, is that a substance can behave very differently when it is taken out of a carrot and put into a tablet.

There are real exceptions to the rule about pills, and the main one is that people who eat no animal foods at all need vitamin B12 from fortified foods or a supplement. Others, such as pregnant women, some older people and those with certain medical conditions, may also need specific supplements, but this depends on the person. Amara writes that the right person to ask is a doctor or a registered dietitian and not an advertisement.

An orange and a glass of orange juice may look similar, but the whole fruit keeps its fibre and fills a person up, while juice holds the sugar with very little of the fibre. A small glass of juice can count as one portion of fruit in many guides, but it should not be the main source, and dried fruit is also sweet and sticky on the teeth. Amara chooses the whole orange, peels it slowly and finds that it lasts far longer than a drink.

At the shop, Amara finds crisps, juice and even biscuits labelled with the word superfood, and Kofi explains that the word has no scientific definition and companies may use it as they wish. Detox products make a similar promise, but the body already cleans itself through the liver and the kidneys, and no drink has been shown to speed that up. Amara laughs and writes a new rule in her notebook, which is to be most doubtful of the loudest claims.

Kofi teaches Amara to read food labels, beginning with the list of ingredients, which starts with whatever there is most of, and then looking at the sugar, salt and portion size. Short lists of ingredients that she recognises are usually a good sign, while long lists with sugar near the top deserve a second look. She is surprised to find that the cereal she has eaten for years is mostly sugar.

Food is important, but Mrs Okoro reminds the class that it is only one part of a protective life. Moving the body every day, sleeping well, avoiding tobacco and staying in touch with friends and doctors all matter as well, and for smoking in particular no diet can make up for it. Amara adds a second page to her project, with a picture of a plate, a pair of trainers and a bed.

On Sunday, Kofi invites the whole family to lunch, and everyone sits around one table and talks for two hours. Eating together tends to make meals slower, calmer and more enjoyable, and a healthy way of eating is much easier to keep up when it is something that people actually enjoy. Amara realises that the happiest part of the project is not on her plate at all.

Amara's little cousin Zane refuses every green food on the table, and Kofi laughs and says that this is perfectly normal. Young children often need to see a new food many times before they will accept it, and patience and small tastes work much better than pressure or bribes. Families with a very fussy child, or one with a health problem, can ask a doctor or dietitian for help.

Amara worries that all this healthy food might be too expensive for ordinary families, so she and Kofi make a shopping list on a small budget. Beans, lentils, oats, carrots, cabbage, frozen vegetables, tinned tomatoes and seasonal fruit are all cheap, and together they make dozens of different meals. She realises that the most expensive foods are not the best ones, and often the opposite is true.

When a person cooks at home from simple ingredients, she decides how much salt, sugar and fat goes into each dish, and she often spends less than on ready meals. It does not have to be elaborate, as Kofi shows with a soup made from an onion, some carrots, lentils and a spoonful of spice that takes only forty minutes. Amara cooks it on her own for her mother one evening, and, to her great pride, nobody has any complaints.

Amara designs her Protection Plate: about half vegetables and fruit, a quarter whole grains, and a quarter protein such as beans, fish, eggs or nuts, with a little olive oil. Her family tries it for a week, and she records what they ate, how much it cost and how everyone felt about it. By Friday her little cousin is eating the carrots, and her mother has asked for the lentil soup recipe.

On the day of the school Science Fair, Amara stands beside her display board in a hall full of volcanoes, magnets and robots. In the middle of her board, in big letters, are the three rules that she has learned: food supports but does not cure, a link is not proof, and the whole pattern matters more than any single food. Visitors stop to read them, a few begin to nod, and she feels her nervousness fade a little.

A judge from the university asks the question that Amara has been waiting for: do these foods really prevent disease? She takes a breath and answers that a good pattern of eating is linked with a lower risk of several illnesses, but that it is a matter of chances and not of promises, and that nobody can honestly guarantee more. The judge smiles, writes something down and says that this is exactly the kind of answer that a scientist ought to give.

When the prizes are announced, Amara's project wins a special award for honest science, and Kofi cheers louder than anyone in the hall. On the walk home he tells her that he has learned something as well, which is that good food does not need big promises, only care, variety and time. He says that he wishes he had known this for all thirty years of his restaurant, and then he decides that it is not too late to teach it to his neighbours.

That evening, Amara and Kofi eat a simple supper of beans, vegetables and rice on the doorstep, and agree that the project has changed how they think about food more than how they cook it. This book gives general information only and is not medical advice, so anyone with a health condition, an allergy, a pregnancy, a child to feed or a medicine to take should ask a doctor first. For everyone else, the next step is small and tasty, which is to add one more colour to tomorrow's plate.
